answer:
1000 SCFM of natural gas is about **1607 Nm³/h**.

This assumes the usual US gas-industry standard of 60 °F and 14.696 psia. Normal conditions for Nm³ are 0 °C and 101.325 kPa. I computed it with the ideal-gas law:

- 1000 ft³/min × 60 = 60,000 ft³/h
- 60,000 ft³/h × 0.0283168 m³/ft³ = 1699.0 m³/h at standard conditions
- 1699.0 × (273.15 K / 288.71 K) × (14.696 / 14.696) = **1607.5 Nm³/h**

So 1 SCFM ≈ 1.607 Nm³/h. The answer depends on which standard the SCFM figure uses:

| SCFM standard | Nm³/h |
|---|---|
| 60 °F, 14.696 psia (most common) | 1607.5 |
| 60 °F, 14.73 psia (AGA / US gas billing) | 1611.2 |
| 68 °F, 14.696 psia | 1583.1 |
| 70 °F, 14.7 psia | 1577.6 |

These values ignore that natural gas is not quite an ideal gas. The compressibility factor Z is close to 1 at both reference conditions, so I expect the error to be well under 0.5%. I did not compute this, because it depends on the gas composition. Treat it as an estimate.
